title: Full beat-by-beat script: overnight SSH triage on jump01 (Terminal.app + Google Sheets + Google Docs in Firefox)

steps.title: Opener
steps.window: The recorder card, then Goal doc (Firefox)
steps.do: Recorder is already running. Read the opener off the recorder card with the cursor still, no pause after "in mind". The recorder then minimises and the Goal doc is on screen. During the last words of the opener, start the cursor sliding up and left toward the yellow minimise button at the top left of the Goal doc window. Keep it moving through the goal sentence, no pause after "blocked". Click the yellow button on the word "Minimising" and narrate the rest live.
say: "Step 1: I will be beginning my task soon. Here is the workflow I have in mind."
"I'm going through last night's failed SSH logins on jump01, to decide what gets blocked."
"Minimising the Goal doc now, my cursor's right up on the yellow button at the top left of its window, and I'm left clicking it, so Terminal gets a clear screen."

steps.title: Terminal first look
steps.do: Move the cursor down and over to the Dock on the left edge, to the Terminal icon. Rest on it until the Terminal label pops up beside it, then click it (Terminal is already open in Documents/Project, so this just brings it forward); pause 1 s after "clicking it". Read the "$ " prompt (16 pt) in Documents/Project. Type wc -l auth-jump01.log while speaking, no pause, then press Return. Read the output line: 59 auth-jump01.log. The log has 59 lines; hold on to that for the import check.
say: "Step 2: Okay, so Terminal first. I'm moving my cursor down and over to the Dock on the left edge, looking for the Terminal icon."
"My cursor's on the Terminal icon now, and the Terminal label pops up beside it. It's already open in the project folder, so I'm clicking it."
"Alright, Terminal comes forward, and I can see the dollar prompt sitting in Documents, Project, so I'm ready to start straight away."
"So now I'm typing in the window, w c, space, dash l, space, and then the log name, auth-jump01.log, because I want a raw line count first to check the sheet import against later."
"Okay, pressing Return to run it, and the count prints just below the prompt."
"So it prints 59 beside auth-jump01.log. That means the log has 59 lines, and I'll hold on to that number for the import check."

steps.title: Count failed and unknown-account logins
steps.do: At the Terminal prompt type grep -c "Failed password" auth-jump01.log and press Return. Read the count on the next line: 53 Failed password lines, the total the pivot has to hit. Right under it type grep -c "invalid user" auth-jump01.log and press Return. Read the second count: 14 invalid user lines (someone guessing usernames). Method to say: use the totals as the bar the pivot must hit if they are clean whole counts; if a count looks off, recheck the grep pattern. Here, 53 and 14 are clean, so they are the bar.
steps.type:
grep -c "Failed password" auth-jump01.log
grep -c "invalid user" auth-jump01.log
say: "Step 3: now the failures. Typing grep, space, dash c, then Failed password in quotes, and the log name, because I want one total of failed logins that the pivot has to match later."
"Pressing Return, and the number comes back just below."
"Okay, it says 53. So that's 53 Failed password lines, and that's the total the pivot has to hit."
"Right below that, I'm typing grep dash c again, this time for invalid user in quotes, and the log name, to count the tries on accounts that don't exist on jump01."
"Pressing Return again, and the second count lands underneath."
"That one's 14. So 14 invalid user lines, and that tells me someone was guessing usernames, not just fumbling a password."
"So let me think about this. Both are clean whole counts, so they're my bar. If the pivot doesn't come to 53, then the import's wrong, and I'd recheck before ranking anything."

steps.title: List successful logins
steps.do: Type grep 'Accepted' auth-jump01.log (Accepted in single quotes) and press Return. Read the six Accepted lines: three publickey (00:30:00, 07:05:00, 07:40:00) and three password (03:52:34 svc_backup from 192.0.2.77, 04:20:34 jsmith from 198.51.100.140, 06:04:12 ops.admin from 10.20.4.11). Rest the cursor on line 2: 03:52:34 Accepted password for svc_backup from 192.0.2.77 (port 62963), and say you will come back to it. Method to say: an IP with failures then Accepted password gets a closer look; IPs with only publickey or no success stay on the failure count. Nothing is blocked from Terminal; those IPs get compared in the sheet.
say: "Step 4: now who got in. I'm typing grep, space, Accepted in single quotes, and the log name on the next line down, so every successful login prints and stands out against the failures."
"Pressing Return, and the Accepted lines print just below the prompt."
"Okay, I count six Accepted lines. Three are publickey and three are password, and it's the password ones I'm after."
"I'm resting my cursor on the second line, 03:52:34, Accepted password for svc_backup from 192.0.2.77. Hmm, that's interesting, I'll come back to it."
"Here's my thinking. An IP that failed, then got in needs its account checked, so I'm not blocking anything from Terminal. I'll compare those IPs in the sheet first."

steps.title: Leave Terminal for the sheet
steps.window: Terminal window, Dock, then Google Sheets (Firefox)
steps.do: Move the cursor up to the top left of the Terminal window and click the yellow minimise button (pause 1 s after "clicking"). Move down the Dock on the left to the minimised sheets window and click it to bring the sheet back. Read Google Sheets in Firefox: the title "jump01 overnight triage" at the top, and a completely empty grid under it.
say: "Step 5: Terminal's done for now. I'm moving my cursor up to the top left of the Terminal window, to the yellow minimise button, and clicking to tuck it away."
"Alright, moving my cursor down the Dock on the left, to the minimised sheets window, and clicking it to bring the sheet back up."
"Google Sheets is up. At the top I can see the title, jump01 overnight triage, and the grid below is completely empty."

steps.title: Import the log export
steps.window: Google Sheets (Firefox) > Import files dialog > macOS file picker
steps.do: Move up to the Sheets menu bar, File on the far left. Click File (pause 1 s after "left click") and move down the list to Import, select it (pause 1 s). In the Import files box click the Upload tab along the top (the file is local, not in Drive). In the middle of the Upload tab click Browse. In the Mac file picker click Documents in the left sidebar, then double-click Project in the list on the right. Click auth-jump01-excerpt.csv (say "excerpt", not the extension) once to select it, then click Open at the bottom right of the picker. In the Import file box, under Import location, click Replace current sheet, then click Import data at the bottom of the box. Wait about a second while the rows fill in. Method to say: Replace if the open sheet is blank and already named; New sheet if it holds anything. Here the sheet was blank and named, so Replace; data, pivot and decisions share one file.
say: "Step 6: getting the export in. So I'm moving my cursor up to the Sheets menu bar, to File on the far left."
"My cursor's on File now, and I'm pressing left click to drop the menu down, because File is where the Import option lives."
"The File menu is open. Now I'm moving my cursor down the list to Import, and selecting it, because I want the data brought into this sheet rather than opening a second file."
"Okay, an Import files box opens with tabs along the top. The file's sitting locally on my Mac, not in Drive, so I'm moving my cursor across and clicking the Upload tab."
"In the middle of the Upload tab there's the Browse button. I'm moving my cursor down onto Browse. Pressing it so I can pick the file myself."
"Now the Mac file picker opens. I'm moving my cursor over to the left sidebar, to Documents, and giving it a click there, because the inputs sit under Documents."
"Okay, Project shows up in the list on the right. I'm moving my cursor across onto Project, and since both inputs live there, I'm double-clicking it."
"Inside Project, the excerpt file sits below. That's the spreadsheet copy of the same 59 log lines. I'm moving my cursor down onto it, and one click selects it."
"Okay, so now I'm moving my cursor down to the bottom right of the picker, and there's the Open button. Clicking it because I want to start the upload of the excerpt."

"Now an Import file box comes up. Under Import location, I'm moving my cursor down the options and picking Replace current sheet. This blank one's already named for the job, so the data can go straight into it."
"Then I'm moving my cursor down to the bottom of the box, to the Import data button. I'll press that to bring the rows into the sheet."
"Okay, just waiting a second while the rows fill in below."
"So why Replace current sheet and not a new sheet? This sheet was blank and already named, so data, pivot and decisions all share one file, right next to their source."

steps.title: Read the columns and count the rows
steps.do: Look across row 1: A timestamp, B host, C event, D user, E invalid_user, F src_ip, G decision. src_ip is column F, the later filter column. Move the cursor over to column G, to look only, without clicking: decision is empty all the way down, the column you fill in yourself. The active cell is still A1, so press Command Down to jump to the bottom of the data. The last row number on the left is 60, timestamp 07:40:00. Check: 60 minus the header row is 59, and Terminal said 59 lines, so they match and nothing was dropped. Press Command Up to return to the top row.
say: "Step 7: checking the import. Looking across row 1 at the top, I can see timestamp, host, event, user, invalid user, src ip and decision. So src ip is in column F, and F's my filter column later."
"Now I'm moving my cursor over to column G on the right, decision, and it's empty all the way down. That's the column I'll be filling in myself."
"The active cell's still A1, so I'm holding Command and pressing the Down arrow, to jump to the bottom of the data."
"Okay, down on the left edge, the last row number is 60, and the timestamp in that row says 07:40:00."
"Sixty minus the header row is 59, and Terminal said 59 lines. They match, so nothing's been dropped in the import."
"Holding Command and pressing the Up arrow, to get back to the top row."

steps.title: Freeze the header and add a filter
steps.do: Move up to the menu bar and across to View. Click View (pause 1 s after "left click"). Move down to Freeze, and a submenu slides out to the right. Move across into the submenu and click 1 row. Then go up to the toolbar, right side, to the Create a filter icon; the Create a filter tooltip shows; click it. Read row 1: a filter icon in every header, A1 across to G1, so the filter is on.
say: "Step 8: I want the header frozen before I scroll. So I'm moving my cursor up to the menu bar and across to View."
"My cursor's on View, and I'm pressing left click to open the list, because the freeze options live under View."
"The View menu is open. Now I'm moving my cursor down to Freeze, and a menu slides out to the right to choose rows."
"I'm moving my cursor across to the right into that submenu, onto 1 row, and clicking it, so the column names stay up top while I scroll."
"Now I'm moving my cursor up to the toolbar, over to the right side, to the Create a filter icon, and the Create a filter tooltip shows. A click on that, so I can filter by IP later."
"Okay, row 1 now shows a filter icon in every header, from A1 across to G1. So the filter is on."

steps.title: Insert the pivot table
steps.window: Google Sheets: Sheet1 > Create pivot table dialog
steps.do: Move the cursor down off the row 1 filter icons onto cell A1 at the top left of the grid and click it (pause 1 s). Press Command A so the whole import is selected. Glance at the name box at the top left: it reads A1:G60. Move back up to the menu bar and across, past View, to Insert; click Insert (pause 1 s). Move down the list to Pivot table and choose it with a left click. In the Create pivot table box in the middle of the screen, click New sheet (pause 1 s), which leaves Sheet1's rows untouched. Move down and right to Create at the bottom right of the box and click it (pause 1 s). Read the bottom tabs: a new tab Pivot Table 1, with the editor open on the right. Method to say: pivot when counts are needed for many IP and event pairs; formulas when only one or two numbers are needed. Here a pivot counts everything at once, where COUNTIF would need a formula per IP and event.
say: "Step 9: okay, the pivot. My cursor's sitting over the filter icons in row 1, so I'm moving it down a touch onto cell A1 itself, top left of the grid, and clicking it, to start the selection there."
"Now pressing Command A on the keyboard, so the whole import's selected in one go."
"Alright, glancing up at the name box, top left, it says A1 to G60, so everything's in."
"So I'm moving my cursor back up to the menu bar and across to the right, past View, to Insert."
"My cursor's up on the menu bar now, and I'm clicking Insert to open the menu, since the pivot table option lives in it."
"The Insert menu is open. Let me move my cursor down the list to Pivot table, and I'm choosing it with a left click, to get one row per IP."
"Okay, a Create pivot table box opens in the middle of the screen. I'm moving my cursor down inside it to New sheet, and left clicking on New sheet, to leave Sheet1's rows untouched."
"Now I'm moving my cursor down and to the right, to the Create button at the bottom right of the box. Pressing it with a left click, so the pivot gets its own tab."
"So down at the bottom, a new tab appears, Pivot Table 1, with the editor open over on the right."
"Let me think. COUNTIF means a formula per IP and event. A pivot counts them all at once, so I'll stick with it."

steps.title: Rows and columns
steps.window: Google Sheets: Pivot Table 1, pivot editor
steps.do: Move over to the pivot editor on the right, down to Rows, and click the Add button beside it (pause 1 s). In the list that drops down, move down to src_ip and click it, so every address gets its own row. Move further down to Columns and click its Add button. In the list, click event. On the Columns card, directly under event, click the Show totals checkbox to untick it (it is ticked; pause 1 s after unticking), because only counts per event type are needed. Read across the header row of the pivot, row 2: B Accepted password, C Accepted publickey, D Failed password.
say: "Step 10: the rows. I'm moving my cursor over to the editor on the right, down to Rows, onto the Add button beside it. Clicking it, because IPs run down the side."
"A list drops down below Add. I'm moving my cursor down that list to src underscore ip and left clicking it, so every address gets its own row."
"Okay, I'm moving my cursor further down the editor to Columns, onto the Add button beside it. Left click there to put event types across the top."
"Another list opens. I'm moving my cursor down to event and selecting it, since it's the type of each try."

"Alright, just below event on the Columns card, my cursor goes to the Show totals checkbox, which is ticked. Unticking it with a left click, because I only need counts per event type, not a total across them."
"So, looking across the header row, row 2, B's Accepted password, C's Accepted publickey, D's Failed password."

steps.title: Values: count the rows
steps.window: Google Sheets: Pivot Table 1, pivot editor
steps.do: Move down the editor to Values and click its Add button (pause 1 s). In the list that opens, move down and pick event. Look lower on the value card at the Summarize by box. If it already says COUNTA, leave it as it is. If it shows SUM, left click the Summarize by dropdown to open it, move down to COUNTA and click it (pause 1 s), since these are words. Method to say: COUNTA when the value field is text; SUM only for numeric fields. Each log line is one attempt, so COUNTA fits. Read the grid on the left: the counts fill in, with a Grand Total on row 9.
say: "Step 11: the counts. I'm moving my cursor down the editor to Values and onto its Add button. Clicking, so I can say what's counted."
"A list opens below. Let me move my cursor down it and pick event, because every row has one."
"Okay, now I'm looking lower on the value card, at the Summarize by box, to see what it's set to."
"Summarize by shows COUNTA already, so I'm leaving it, or if it shows SUM I'm clicking that dropdown and moving down to COUNTA."
"Then moving down to COUNTA and clicking it, since these are words."
"Okay, each line's one attempt, so COUNTA fits. It counts the text entries, which is what I need."
"Alright, looking left at the grid, the counts fill in, with a Grand Total on row 9."

steps.title: Sort by failures
steps.window: Google Sheets: Pivot Table 1, pivot editor
steps.do: Move back up to the Rows card, down to Order, and open that dropdown with a left click; choose Descending (pause 1 s). Directly under it, on the same card, click the Sort by dropdown, move down the list and pick Failed password (pause 1 s), so the most failures are on top. Read down rows 3 to 8: 203.0.113.45 18, 198.51.100.23 14, 192.0.2.77 9, 198.51.100.140 7, 10.20.4.11 3 (say it as the ten-dot address), 192.0.2.200 2. Method to say: descending by Failed password when risk is driven by attempt volume; by time if the question were order of events. Here you work down from the biggest risk. Move up to the top right of the editor and click the close icon (pause 1 s) to get the full sheet back.
say: "Step 12: noisiest first. I'm moving my cursor back up to the Rows card, down to Order, opening that dropdown with a left click and choosing Descending, to lead with big numbers."
"Just below it is Sort by. I'm left clicking that dropdown, moving down the list, and picking Failed password, to put the most failures on top."
"So, sorted like this, I'll work down from the biggest risk."
"Now I'm moving my cursor up to the top right of the editor, to the close icon. Clicking it to get the full sheet back."

steps.title: Check the pivot total against Terminal
steps.do: Move the cursor left onto the grid and down to the bottom of column D. Click D9 (pause 1 s). Read it: 53 failures. Check it against Terminal: the pivot says 53 and grep said 53, so they match and nothing is missing. Look just left of it: B9 and C9 are 3 each, password and publickey, the same as Terminal.
say: "Step 13: a check against Terminal. I'm moving my cursor left onto the grid, down to the bottom of column D. Clicking D9, to read the failure total."
"Okay, with my cursor on D9, it reads 53 failures."
"So the pivot says 53, and grep said 53 back in Terminal. They match, so nothing's missing."
"Looking just left of it, B9 and C9 are 3 each, password and publickey, same as Terminal."

steps.title: Read the ranking
steps.do: Move the cursor up onto rows 3 and 4 in column D: 203.0.113.45 has 18 and 198.51.100.23 has 14, the biggest risk. Move down to rows 5 and 6: in column D, 192.0.2.77 has 9 failures and over in column B it has 1 accepted password; 198.51.100.140 has 7 and 1 the same way, so both got in after failing. Then rows 7 and 8, which are small: for the ten-dot address (10.20.4.11), columns B, C and D read 1, 3 and 3, and 192.0.2.200 has just 2 in D.
say: "Step 14: the ranking. My cursor's up on rows 3 and 4 in column D, 203.0.113.45 has 18 and 198.51.100.23 has 14. They're the biggest risk."

"Now I'm moving my cursor down to rows 5 and 6. In column D, 192.0.2.77 has 9 failures, and over in column B it has 1 accepted password. 198.51.100.140 has 7 and 1 the same way, so both got in after failing."
"Then down to rows 7 and 8, which are small. For the ten-dot address, columns B, C and D read 1, 3 and 3, and 192.0.2.200 has just 2 in D."

steps.title: Decision column header
steps.do: Move right, past the Failed password column, to cell E2 and click it (pause 1 s) so decisions sit beside the counts. Type Decision in E2 while speaking, no pause. Press Return to drop the cursor down to E3.
say: "Step 15: a decision column. I'm moving my cursor right, past the Failed password column, to E2, and clicking there, so decisions sit beside counts."
"Okay, typing Decision in E2, so it's clear what the column's for."
"Now hitting Return on the keyboard, to drop the cursor down to E3."

steps.title: Dropdown chips
steps.window: Google Sheets: Pivot Table 1 > Data validation panel
steps.do: Move down from E2 to E3, beside 203.0.113.45, and click it (pause 1 s); the range has to start on the first IP. Hold Shift and press Down five times so E3:E8 is selected, and read the name box: E3:E8. Move back up to the menu bar, over to Insert, click it (pause 1 s), go down the list to Dropdown and select it (pause 1 s). The Data validation panel opens on the right: click into the Option 1 box and type Block. Click Add another item under the Option 1 box (pause 1 s), and in Option 2 type Watch. Click Add another item again (pause 1 s), and in Option 3 type Ignore. Click Done at the bottom of the panel (pause 1 s) to save the choices to E3:E8. Method to say: dropdown when the cell must be counted later; free text only for notes. Here fixed words, because COUNTIF needs exact matches. Read E3:E8: each has a chip now.
say: "Step 16: the choices. I'm moving my cursor down from E2 to E3, beside 203.0.113.45, and a click there, because the range starts on the first IP."
"Now holding Shift and pressing Down five times, so E3 to E8 is selected."
"The name box up top says E3 to E8."
"Moving my cursor back up to the menu bar, over to Insert."
"My cursor's on Insert, and I'm clicking, since Dropdown's in that menu."
"Then down the list to Dropdown, and selecting it, for fixed words."
"A Data validation panel opens on the right. I'm clicking into the Option 1 box and typing Block."
"I'm moving my cursor below, to Add another item. Hitting it for a second box."
"In Option 2 underneath, typing Watch, the middle ground."
"Then lower down, Add another item once more, pressing it for a third box."
"In Option 3, typing Ignore."
"Now down to Done at the bottom of the panel. Clicking it to save the choices."
"Fixed words, because COUNTIF needs exact matches."
"Looking down E3 to E8, each cell has a chip now."

steps.title: Filter, read and mark 203.0.113.45
steps.window: Google Sheets: Sheet1 filter, then Pivot Table 1
steps.do: 1. Move down to the sheet tabs at the very bottom and click Sheet1 at the bottom left (pause 1 s); the decision needs raw rows, not just counts. 2. Go up to row 1, across to F1, and click its filter icon at the right edge of the cell (pause 1 s). 3. In the filter panel, under Filter by values, press Clear (pause 1 s). 4. Scroll down the value list, tick 203.0.113.45 (pause 1 s), then click OK at the bottom right of the panel (pause 1 s). 5. Read the filtered rows: only 203.0.113.45, and every one a Failed password. 6. Read across: column D is root and admin over and over, column E says no on every row, timestamps 01:12:00 to 01:16:05, and nothing Accepted. 7. Say your own evidence from the rows and your own verdict for this IP. Your goal's first rule: an outside IP with 5+ failures, real admin names tried and no success is a Block. 8. Move back down to the tabs and click Pivot Table 1, just right of Sheet1 (pause 1 s). 9. Move over to column E, to E3 next to 203.0.113.45, and click its chip (pause 1 s). 10. Pick the chip word that matches the verdict you said. The line you speak here reads Block. 11. Say what E3 now shows.
say: "Step 17: before deciding on the top IP, I want its raw lines. So I'm moving my cursor down to the sheet tabs at the very bottom of the window."
"My cursor's on Sheet1, at the bottom left, and I'm clicking that tab, because the decision needs raw rows, not just counts."
"Okay, now up to row 1 and across to F1, and I'm clicking its filter icon at the right edge of the cell, since that's my filter column."
"The filter panel opens below it. I'm moving my cursor down to Filter by values, and I press Clear, so nothing's ticked."
"Then scrolling down the value list to 203.0.113.45, and ticking it, so only its rows come back."
"Now down to the OK button at the bottom right of the panel, and I'm going to left click on it to apply."
"Alright, just this IP now. The filtered rows are all 203.0.113.45, and every one is a Failed password."
"Reading across, column D is root and admin over and over, and column E says no on every row, from 01:12:00 to 01:16:05, with nothing Accepted."
"Putting it together: [say the evidence from the rows]. Real admin names from outside, and never in. That makes this one [say the decision]."
"So I'm moving my cursor back down to the tabs, to Pivot Table 1, just right of Sheet1."
"Clicking the Pivot Table 1 tab now with a left click, so the decision goes beside the count."
"Okay, I'm moving my cursor over to column E, to E3, next to 203.0.113.45, and clicking its chip, so the decision lands on the right row."
"The list opens under the chip, and I'm moving my cursor down to Block and picking it, to match what I said."
"So E3 now shows Block."

steps.title: Filter, read and mark 198.51.100.23
steps.window: Google Sheets: Sheet1 filter, then Pivot Table 1
steps.do: 1. Move down to the sheet tabs at the bottom and click Sheet1 at the bottom left (pause 1 s). 2. Go up to F1 and click the filter icon at the cell's right edge so the value list opens (pause 1 s). 3. Under Filter by values press Clear first (pause 1 s). 4. Scan the value list for each of 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.140 and 192.0.2.200 and tick each one; the list is not in that order (pause 1 s after ticking). Only these three are left. 5. Click OK at the bottom right of the panel (pause 1 s). 6. Read their rows: 198.51.100.23 has 14 failures, 198.51.100.140 has 7, 192.0.2.200 just 2. 7. Read across: 198.51.100.23 is all invalid users, test, ubuntu, oracle, nothing Accepted. Further down, 198.51.100.140 has jsmith failing and then getting in at 04:20:34. 192.0.2.200 has root twice, at 05:30:00 and 05:31:00. 8. Say your own verdict for each IP, in that order: 198.51.100.23, then 198.51.100.140, then 192.0.2.200. Rule 1 of your goal gives Block for an outside IP with 5+ failures on accounts that do not exist and no success. 9. Move back down to the tabs and click Pivot Table 1 (pause 1 s). 10. Move over to column E, to E4 beside 198.51.100.23, and click its chip (pause 1 s). Pick the chip word that matches the verdict you said. The lines you speak here name Block for this one. 11. Move down two rows to E6 beside 198.51.100.140, click its chip and pick the word for your verdict; the line you speak reads Watch. 12. Down again to E8 beside 192.0.2.200, click its chip and pick the word for your verdict; the line you speak reads Ignore. 13. Read E4, E6 and E8: each has its word, and E3 above keeps its own.
say: "Step 18: okay, the other three together, 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.140 and 192.0.2.200. I'm moving my cursor down to the sheet tabs at the bottom."
"Sheet1 is at the bottom left, and I'm going in with a left click on it, since the rows are what I judge from."
"Then up to F1, to the filter icon at the cell's right edge, clicking so the value list opens."
"In the panel below, under Filter by values, I press Clear first, so the last IP's unticked too."
"Then I'm moving down the list, ticking 198.51.100.23 and 198.51.100.140, and for 192.0.2.200 I'm ticking it too, so only these three are left."
"OK at the bottom right of the panel, and I'm clicking to filter."
"Their rows only. 198.51.100.23 has 14 failures, 198.51.100.140 has 7, and 192.0.2.200 just 2."

"Looking across, 198.51.100.23 is all invalid users, test, ubuntu, oracle, nothing Accepted. Further down, 198.51.100.140 has jsmith failing and then getting in at 04:20:34. And 192.0.2.200 has root twice, at 05:30:00 and 05:31:00."

"Weighing it up: 198.51.100.23, 14 failures on accounts that don't exist, [say the decision]. 198.51.100.140, 7 failures and then a login, [say the decision]. And 192.0.2.200, just 2 tries, [say the decision]."
"Now I'm moving my cursor back down to the tabs, towards Pivot Table 1 on the right of Sheet1."
"Left click on the Pivot Table 1 tab, to record those decisions beside their counts."
"Okay, I'm moving my cursor over to column E, to E4, beside 198.51.100.23."
"My cursor's on the E4 chip beside 198.51.100.23, so I'm clicking it, and from the list below I'll choose Block."
"Now I'm moving my cursor down two rows to E6, beside 198.51.100.140, left clicking its chip, and picking Watch from the list."
"Then down again to E8, beside 192.0.2.200, a click on its chip, and I'm picking Ignore from the list that opens."
"E4, E6 and E8 have their words now, and E3 above still keeps its own."

steps.title: Filter, read and mark 192.0.2.77

steps.title: Per-IP failures from the raw log
steps.do: Full command: grep 'Failed password' auth-jump01.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn  Typed in two parts. In the Terminal window type grep 'Failed password' auth-jump01.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' (grep Failed password, then the log name, piped to awk, the fourth field from the end, because invalid user lines are longer so a fixed field would grab the wrong word). Continue on the same line with  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn (leading space), so each IP gets a count, biggest first. Press Return. Read the counts under the prompt: 18 203.0.113.45, 14 198.51.100.23, 9 192.0.2.77, 7 198.51.100.140, 3 for the ten-dot address (10.20.4.11), 2 192.0.2.200. Method to say: $(NF-3) when lines differ in word count (invalid user lines add words); a fixed field only when every line has the same shape. Counting from the raw log, not the sheet, means an import slip would show. Check those six against D3:D8 in the pivot, 18, 14, 9, 7, 3, 2: all match.
steps.type: grep 'Failed password' auth-jump01.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
